MCSC-101.title: Asymptotic analysis and structures
MCSC-101.explanation: Big-O bounds growth from above; amortised analysis bounds an average over a worst-case sequence. Fibonacci heaps support efficient amortised decrease-key; splay trees move accessed nodes towards the root; dynamic trees represent changing forests.
MCSC-101.example: Repeated accesses to a splay tree can become cheaper as frequently used nodes move near the root.
MCSC-101.distinction: Worst-case cost concerns one operation; amortised cost applies to a sequence, without assuming random inputs.

MCSC-101.title: Network flows
MCSC-101.explanation: A feasible flow obeys edge capacities and conservation at intermediate vertices. The maximum-flow minimum-cut theorem equates maximum source-to-sink flow with the capacity of a smallest cut; minimum-cost flow also accounts for edge costs.
MCSC-101.example: For one source-to-sink path with capacities 3 and 2, at most 2 units can flow.
MCSC-101.distinction: Maximum flow optimises volume; minimum-cost flow optimises cost subject to required flow and capacities.

MCSC-101.title: Linear and semidefinite programming
MCSC-101.explanation: A linear programme optimises a linear objective under linear equalities and inequalities. Semidefinite programming generalises this using a positive semidefinite matrix constraint, useful for relaxations.
MCSC-101.example: Maximise 3x+2y subject to x+y≤4 and x,y≥0: allocating all 4 units to x gives objective 12.
MCSC-101.distinction: Integer constraints make a linear model discrete; its continuous relaxation can give a bound rather than a feasible integer solution.

MCSC-101.title: Approximation and intractability
MCSC-101.explanation: A polynomial-time approximation algorithm trades exact optimality for a proven quality guarantee on hard optimisation problems. The ratio is defined relative to an optimum and depends on whether the problem is minimisation or maximisation.
MCSC-101.example: A maximal matching gives a vertex cover with at most twice as many vertices as an optimal cover.
MCSC-101.distinction: An approximation guarantee is a proven bound; a heuristic may work well but need not offer one.

MCSC-101.title: Large data and randomisation
MCSC-101.explanation: Streaming algorithms use limited memory and often one pass. Compression represents data economically; compressed sensing recovers structured sparse signals under suitable measurement assumptions. Randomised algorithms use random choices with a stated success or runtime guarantee.
MCSC-101.example: Reservoir sampling maintains a uniform random sample from a stream of unknown length.
MCSC-101.distinction: Monte Carlo algorithms allow bounded error; Las Vegas algorithms are correct when they terminate but have random runtime.

MCSC-101.title: Geometry, parallelism and lab methods
MCSC-101.explanation: Computational geometry studies geometric objects and queries; parallel algorithms split work while accounting for synchronisation. The syllabus lab also includes search, sorting, linked lists, trees, BFS/DFS, spanning trees, string matching, greedy methods, dynamic programming and backtracking.
MCSC-101.example: Breadth-first search explores levels with a queue; depth-first search follows branches using a stack or recursion.
MCSC-101.distinction: Parallel speedup depends on serial work and communication, not simply the processor count.

MCSC-101.title: Residual graphs and augmenting paths
MCSC-101.explanation: A residual graph represents how much flow can still be sent or reversed on each edge. Ford–Fulkerson repeatedly finds an augmenting path and increases flow by its smallest residual capacity until no augmenting path remains.
MCSC-101.example: If a path has residual capacities 5, 2 and 4, its bottleneck is 2; augmenting by 2 saturates at least one edge.
MCSC-101.distinction: Reverse residual edges allow earlier choices to be revised; they are not necessarily original network edges.

MCSC-101.title: Complexity and reductions
MCSC-101.explanation: A decision problem asks a yes/no question. A polynomial-time reduction transforms one problem into another, showing that an efficient solution to the second would solve the first; NP-completeness combines membership in NP with NP-hardness.
MCSC-101.example: To show problem B is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem A to B and prove that yes-instances correspond.
MCSC-101.distinction: A reduction from A to B supports B being at least as hard as A; the direction matters.

MCSC-101.title: Dynamic programming and greedy strategies
MCSC-101.explanation: Dynamic programming stores solutions to overlapping subproblems and combines them using a recurrence. A greedy algorithm chooses a locally appealing step and needs a proof that those choices lead to an optimal result.
MCSC-101.example: For 0/1 knapsack, compare excluding an item with including it when capacity permits, using the preceding item row.
MCSC-101.distinction: A plausible greedy rule is not enough: 0/1 knapsack is not generally solved optimally by sorting items by value-to-weight ratio.

MCSC-101.title: Min-cost flow and circulation
MCSC-101.explanation: A min-cost flow problem assigns a cost per unit of flow to each directed edge and asks for a feasible flow of minimum total cost. A circulation requires conservation at every vertex; supplies, demands and lower bounds can be incorporated by an appropriate transformation. Negative-cost cycles matter because pushing flow around one may reduce the objective.
MCSC-101.example: Sending three units along a path of per-unit costs 2 and 1 costs 3 × (2+1) = 9, provided both edges have capacity at least three. A cheaper path may become unavailable when its capacity is exhausted.
MCSC-101.distinction: Maximum flow maximises how much reaches the sink; min-cost flow chooses a least-cost feasible allocation for a specified demand or objective.

MCSC-101.title: Approximation: vertex cover worked example
MCSC-101.explanation: A vertex cover contains at least one endpoint of every edge. Repeatedly choose an uncovered edge, add both endpoints to the cover and remove their incident edges. The chosen edges form a matching; any cover needs at least one endpoint per chosen edge, so selecting both gives a cover no larger than twice the optimum.
MCSC-101.example: For edges AB and BC, selecting AB adds A and B and covers both edges. The returned cover has size 2; {B} is an optimal cover of size 1.
MCSC-101.distinction: The factor 2 is a worst-case guarantee, not a prediction that every output is twice optimal.

MCSC-104.title: Learning and validation
MCSC-104.explanation: Supervised learning estimates a mapping from labelled examples; unsupervised learning finds structure without target labels. Training fits parameters, validation selects a model, and a held-out test estimates final generalisation.
MCSC-104.example: In five-fold cross-validation, train on four folds and validate on the fifth, rotating until every fold has served as validation.
MCSC-104.distinction: Fit preprocessing only within each training fold to avoid leakage from validation data.

MCSC-104.title: Covariance, correlation and regression
MCSC-104.explanation: Covariance indicates joint variation; correlation standardises it. Linear regression predicts a continuous target as an intercept plus a weighted sum of features, often fitted by least squares.
MCSC-104.example: For y=2+3x, x=4 gives a prediction of 14; residuals are observed values minus predictions.
MCSC-104.distinction: Correlation measures linear association, not causation; multiple regression uses several predictors.

MCSC-104.title: Principal component analysis
MCSC-104.explanation: PCA centres data and identifies orthogonal directions of maximum variance using eigenvectors of a covariance matrix or singular value decomposition. Retaining a few components can reduce dimension.
MCSC-104.example: Highly correlated height and weight variables may largely vary along a single diagonal component.
MCSC-104.distinction: Feature selection retains original variables; PCA creates new combinations. Scale matters when units differ.

MCSC-104.title: Clustering
MCSC-104.explanation: Clustering groups similar examples using a distance or density criterion. k-means alternates assignments and centroid updates; hierarchical clustering builds nested groups; density methods identify dense regions and noise.
MCSC-104.example: With points near 1, 2 and 10, a two-centre solution may group 1 and 2 separately from 10.
MCSC-104.distinction: k-means requires a chosen k and favours compact groups; density-based methods can discover irregular shapes.

MCSC-104.title: Classification and feature selection
MCSC-104.explanation: A classifier predicts labels. k-nearest neighbours votes among nearby training examples; naive Bayes combines class priors and feature likelihoods under conditional independence; support vector machines seek a separating margin.
MCSC-104.example: A 3-nearest-neighbour classifier with labels A, A, B predicts A for a new point.
MCSC-104.distinction: Distance-based methods are sensitive to scaling; naive Bayes can work despite imperfect independence assumptions.

MCSC-104.title: Trees, ensembles and model quality
MCSC-104.explanation: Decision trees split features into regions; boosting sequentially combines weak learners. Bias describes systematic error while variance describes sensitivity to the training sample.
MCSC-104.example: A decision tree might split on attendance and then assignment score to predict a category.
MCSC-104.distinction: Cross-validation helps tune complexity, while a final untouched test set gives a less biased final assessment.

MCSC-104.title: Cross-validation and data leakage
MCSC-104.explanation: Cross-validation repeatedly fits and evaluates on different training and validation folds. Scaling, feature selection and imputation must be learned inside each training fold to avoid using validation information.
MCSC-104.example: In five-fold validation, fit a scaler on four folds, transform the held-out fold using those parameters, and repeat for each fold.
MCSC-104.distinction: A test set is reserved for final evaluation; repeatedly selecting models on it turns it into validation data.

MCSC-104.title: Naive Bayes and class imbalance
MCSC-104.explanation: Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ rule with a conditional-independence assumption between features given the class. For imbalanced data, report class-specific precision and recall rather than accuracy alone.
MCSC-104.example: If 100 cases contain 5 positives, predicting every case negative gives 95% accuracy but zero recall for the positive class.
MCSC-104.distinction: Precision asks how many predicted positives are correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found.

MCSC-104.title: Bias, variance and boosting
MCSC-104.explanation: A model with high bias may underfit, while a high-variance model can fit noise and change substantially across datasets. Boosting combines weak learners sequentially to improve a chosen objective.
MCSC-104.example: A shallow tree ensemble can correct patterns missed by earlier trees, but excessive fitting to noise can still hurt held-out performance.
MCSC-104.distinction: Bagging fits models largely in parallel on resampled data; boosting fits a sequence where later learners address earlier errors.

MCSC-104.title: k-nearest neighbours worked example
MCSC-104.explanation: k-nearest neighbours compares a new observation with training points under a chosen distance. For classification, neighbours vote; for regression, their target values may be averaged. Scaling, k and the distance metric materially affect the result, so they should be selected without using the final test set.
MCSC-104.example: For a new point with three nearest labels A, A and B, majority-vote 3-NN predicts A. With k=1, the prediction is simply the closest point’s label.
MCSC-104.distinction: k-NN is supervised: it uses known targets. k-means is an unsupervised clustering procedure and does not use class labels.

MCSC-104.title: Principal components and explained variance
MCSC-104.explanation: PCA identifies orthogonal directions that successively capture variance in centred data. If covariance eigenvalues are λ₁,…,λₚ, the proportion of variance explained by component i is λᵢ divided by their sum, provided the total variance is positive. Standardising features changes the problem when units differ.
MCSC-104.example: If two eigenvalues are 3 and 1, the first component explains 3/(3+1)=75% of total variance.
MCSC-104.distinction: A component that explains much input variance is not automatically the most predictive direction for a labelled task.

MCSC-201.title: IoT architecture and devices
MCSC-201.explanation: The Internet of Things connects sensing or actuating devices, networks, services and applications. A typical path runs from a sensor through a gateway to storage and a dashboard.
MCSC-201.example: A soil-moisture sensor sends readings to a gateway, which displays trends and can trigger irrigation.
MCSC-201.distinction: A microcontroller such as an Arduino-class board is typically resource constrained; a Raspberry Pi-class computer runs a fuller operating system.

MCSC-201.title: Networking and Linux
MCSC-201.explanation: IP addressing and subnetting group network interfaces; switches forward frames locally, routers connect networks, and access points provide wireless connectivity. Linux exposes network interfaces and device files to software.
MCSC-201.example: A gateway can bridge sensor traffic to a LAN while a router forwards traffic to a remote service.
MCSC-201.distinction: A hub repeats traffic; a switch forwards frames based on learned addresses. Device-file permissions affect access.

MCSC-201.title: Communication and protocols
MCSC-201.explanation: MQTT uses brokered publish–subscribe messaging; CoAP uses lightweight request–response messaging; HTTP supports widely used web APIs. 6LoWPAN adapts IPv6 packets to constrained low-power networks.
MCSC-201.example: A temperature sensor publishes to a broker topic and a dashboard subscribes to that topic.
MCSC-201.distinction: MQTT decouples publisher from subscriber; HTTP commonly uses direct client–server requests.

MCSC-201.title: Web services and data storage
MCSC-201.explanation: A server receives device messages, validates them and stores observations. Relational tables suit structured records and joins; document databases can hold flexible JSON-like records.
MCSC-201.example: A reading record can contain device ID, time, value and unit; a dashboard requests a time range.
MCSC-201.distinction: JSON is a data format; MySQL and MongoDB are databases with different data models.

MCSC-201.title: Security and privacy
MCSC-201.explanation: Identify devices, authenticate requests, encrypt suitable traffic, protect credentials and apply updates. Minimise collected data and design for failure, physical access and device lifecycle.
MCSC-201.example: A compromised sensor should not be able to issue administrator commands; assign it only the permissions it needs.
MCSC-201.distinction: Encryption protects confidentiality in transit, while authorisation controls permitted actions.

MCSC-201.title: Applications and laboratory
MCSC-201.explanation: IoT supports monitoring, remote control, industrial systems, agriculture and healthcare. Evaluate accuracy, latency, availability, energy and safety for the use case.
MCSC-201.example: A greenhouse sensor samples periodically; compare measured temperature against a calibrated reference before automating control.
MCSC-201.distinction: Monitoring observes conditions; closed-loop control acts and observes the result. Validate sensor calibration and failure behaviour.

MCSC-201.title: Addressing, subnetting and routing
MCSC-201.explanation: An IPv4 subnet mask identifies the network prefix and host portion. A router forwards packets between networks using routes; a switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network.
MCSC-201.example: A /24 IPv4 prefix contains 256 addresses in total; usable host-address conventions depend on the subnet and network context.
MCSC-201.distinction: A MAC address identifies a link-layer interface on a local link; an IP address supports network-layer addressing and routing.

MCSC-201.title: MQTT quality of service and device lifecycle
MCSC-201.explanation: MQTT connects clients through a broker and offers delivery levels: QoS 0 at most once, QoS 1 at least once, and QoS 2 exactly once at the MQTT protocol level.
MCSC-201.example: A sensor using QoS 1 may cause a duplicate message after retransmission, so an application should handle duplicates appropriately.
MCSC-201.distinction: A protocol delivery guarantee does not ensure a physical sensor reading is accurate or an actuator performed an action.

MCSC-201.title: IoT data quality and resilience
MCSC-201.explanation: Sensor systems must consider calibration, timestamps, missing readings, power loss, connectivity interruptions and safe update procedures. Analyse end-to-end delay rather than network latency alone.
MCSC-201.example: A gateway can timestamp readings, buffer a bounded number while offline and transmit them after reconnecting, while preserving their original observation times.
MCSC-201.distinction: A measurement may be unavailable, stale or invalid; these states should not silently become zero.

MCSC-201.title: MQTT topics, delivery and retained messages
MCSC-201.explanation: MQTT uses clients and a broker: publishers send messages to topics, and subscribers request topic filters. QoS 0, 1 and 2 express different protocol-level delivery semantics; retained messages allow a broker to store the latest retained message for a topic subject to broker configuration.
MCSC-201.example: A sensor publishes a temperature reading to campus/room1/temp; a monitoring client subscribes to campus/room1/temp and receives matching publications through the broker.
MCSC-201.distinction: QoS 1 permits duplicates. QoS 2 addresses exactly-once delivery at the protocol exchange level, not guaranteed correct sensor readings or safe physical actuation.

MCSC-201.title: 6LoWPAN and constrained networking
MCSC-201.explanation: 6LoWPAN adapts IPv6 to low-power networks with constrained frame sizes. It supports mechanisms such as header compression and fragmentation when needed; the exact link and deployment determine achievable reliability and performance.
MCSC-201.example: A small sensor network can use an adaptation layer to carry IPv6 traffic over a constrained link, while a border router connects it with a wider IP network.
MCSC-201.distinction: 6LoWPAN is an adaptation layer; MQTT and CoAP are application-layer protocols serving different messaging needs.

MMLC-201.title: Artificial neurons and network architectures
MMLC-201.explanation: An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation. Feed-forward networks pass information forward; recurrent networks also use state from earlier steps.
MMLC-201.example: For weights 0.5 and 1, inputs 2 and 1, and bias 0, the pre-activation is 2.
MMLC-201.distinction: Biological neurons inspire the abstraction, but an artificial neuron is a simplified mathematical model.

MMLC-201.title: Training and backpropagation
MMLC-201.explanation: A loss measures prediction error. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute gradients; an optimiser adjusts weights to reduce loss on training data.
MMLC-201.example: With loss (w−3)² at w=1, its gradient is −4. A small gradient-descent step increases w towards 3.
MMLC-201.distinction: Training error measures fitted data; validation error helps reveal poor generalisation.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy sets and membership
MMLC-201.explanation: A fuzzy set assigns membership in [0,1], expressing degree of membership in a specified set. Membership functions can be triangular, trapezoidal or other shapes.
MMLC-201.example: A temperature of 28°C might have membership 0.6 in the set warm, depending on the chosen function.
MMLC-201.distinction: Fuzzy membership expresses graded belonging; probability represents uncertainty about an event.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy inference and control
MMLC-201.explanation: Rules combine fuzzy premises and conclusions, such as IF temperature is high THEN fan speed is fast. Fuzzification maps inputs to memberships; inference combines rules; defuzzification produces a crisp output.
MMLC-201.example: A controller can combine warm and hot memberships to produce an intermediate fan setting.
MMLC-201.distinction: A fuzzy rule system represents expert rules; a neural network learns parameters from data.

MMLC-201.title: Genetic algorithms
MMLC-201.explanation: Genetic algorithms evolve candidate solutions using selection, crossover and mutation, guided by a fitness function. Encoding determines how a candidate is represented.
MMLC-201.example: A bit string can encode a subset of features; selection favours candidates with good validation fitness and mutation flips occasional bits.
MMLC-201.distinction: Crossover recombines parents; mutation introduces variation. Neither guarantees a global optimum.

MMLC-201.title: Deep models and regularisation
MMLC-201.explanation: Deep feed-forward networks, CNNs, RNNs and deep belief networks learn different representations. Dropout and other regularisers can reduce overfitting; model selection requires separate validation.
MMLC-201.example: A CNN shares filters over an image, while an RNN processes a sequence with a recurring hidden state.
MMLC-201.distinction: Dropout is a training technique, whereas a CNN is an architectural family.

MMLC-201.title: Perceptron and linear separability
MMLC-201.explanation: A perceptron applies a threshold to a weighted sum. The perceptron learning rule adjusts weights after a misclassification; a single-layer linear decision boundary cannot represent every Boolean function.
MMLC-201.example: The AND function is linearly separable, but XOR is not separable by one straight line in its two-dimensional binary input space.
MMLC-201.distinction: A multilayer network with nonlinear hidden units can represent functions that a single linear threshold unit cannot.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy membership and defuzzification
MMLC-201.explanation: A membership function maps an input to a degree from 0 to 1. Fuzzy inference combines rule activations and an output membership shape; defuzzification converts that result to a crisp action.
MMLC-201.example: A triangular membership function with vertices (20,0), (25,1), (30,0) gives membership 0.6 at 27.
MMLC-201.distinction: A fuzzy membership of 0.6 is a degree of belonging to a chosen set, not necessarily a 60% probability.

MMLC-201.title: Genetic representation and selection
MMLC-201.explanation: A genetic algorithm encodes each candidate, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and iterates. Representation, fitness and constraints determine what solutions are searchable.
MMLC-201.example: To select three features from a set of ten, use a ten-bit string and penalise or repair candidates that do not contain exactly three ones.
MMLC-201.distinction: Mutation introduces variation; selection changes which candidates contribute to later generations.

MMLC-201.title: Perceptron prediction and learning
MMLC-201.explanation: A perceptron computes z=w·x+b and applies a threshold to obtain a binary decision. In the classical update, weights are adjusted when a training example is misclassified. A single linear threshold unit cannot solve a non-linearly separable task such as XOR.
MMLC-201.example: With x=(1,1), w=(0.5,0.5) and b=−0.75, z=0.25; using threshold z≥0 predicts the positive class.
MMLC-201.distinction: A multilayer network adds hidden transformations and nonlinear activations; it can represent decision boundaries a single linear perceptron cannot.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy rules and centroid defuzzification
MMLC-201.explanation: A fuzzy controller typically fuzzifies a crisp input, applies rules using a chosen inference method, aggregates resulting output sets and defuzzifies to obtain an action. For a continuous output membership μ(y), the centroid is ∫yμ(y)dy / ∫μ(y)dy when the denominator is nonzero.
MMLC-201.example: If an aggregated output membership is symmetric around fan speed 50 and has nonzero area, its centroid is 50 in the chosen speed units.
MMLC-201.distinction: A fuzzy membership degree describes belonging to a defined set; it is not necessarily a probability.

MCSE-202.title: Data, samples and bias
MCSE-202.explanation: Data science frames a question, collects data, analyses it and communicates conclusions. A population includes all units of interest; a sample is the subset observed. Selection and measurement bias can distort conclusions.
MCSE-202.example: An online survey about internet use excludes people without access, so its sample may not represent the whole population.
MCSE-202.distinction: Random sampling addresses selection mechanisms; a large but biased sample is not automatically representative.

MCSE-202.title: Summary statistics and exploratory analysis
MCSE-202.explanation: Mean, median, spread and quantiles describe distributions. Histograms, scatter plots and box plots reveal shape, outliers and relationships before modelling.
MCSE-202.example: For 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, the mean is 22 but the median is 3, illustrating sensitivity to an outlier.
MCSE-202.distinction: A histogram shows a distribution; a scatter plot shows pairs of numerical values.

MCSE-202.title: Probability and inference
MCSE-202.explanation: Conditional probability describes an event given evidence. Bayes’ rule combines a prior with a likelihood; intervals and hypothesis tests quantify uncertainty under assumptions.
MCSE-202.example: If P(A)=0.5, P(B|A)=0.8 and P(B)=0.5, Bayes’ rule gives P(A|B)=0.8.
MCSE-202.distinction: A confidence interval is a procedure with long-run coverage, not automatically a posterior probability about a fixed parameter.

MCSE-202.title: Association, confounding and Simpson’s paradox
MCSE-202.explanation: Association does not by itself establish causation. A confounder affects both an exposure and an outcome; Simpson’s paradox occurs when an aggregate trend reverses or changes across groups.
MCSE-202.example: Treatment success can appear lower overall if the treated group contains more severe cases, despite higher success within each severity group.
MCSE-202.distinction: Stratification can reveal group differences; causal conclusions still need a justified design and assumptions.

MCSE-202.title: Regression and predictive models
MCSE-202.explanation: Linear regression predicts a numeric outcome. k-nearest neighbours predicts from nearby examples; naive Bayes estimates class probabilities; k-means groups unlabelled data.
MCSE-202.example: A model can estimate house price from area and location, but it must be evaluated on homes not used for fitting.
MCSE-202.distinction: k-nearest neighbours is supervised when trained with labels; k-means is an unsupervised clustering method.

MCSE-202.title: Bayesian modelling and communication
MCSE-202.explanation: Bayesian inference updates a prior distribution using data likelihood to obtain a posterior. Hierarchical models share information across groups while allowing group-level differences.
MCSE-202.example: A prior for each district’s rate can be linked to a common population distribution, then updated with district observations.
MCSE-202.distinction: Posterior uncertainty depends on the model and prior; diagnostic plots and clear uncertainty reporting remain essential.

MCSE-202.title: Simpson’s paradox and group composition
MCSE-202.explanation: An association in aggregate data can reverse after dividing data into relevant groups, because the group mix differs. Inspect denominators and group-level rates before interpreting a summary.
MCSE-202.example: Treatment A succeeds in 9/10 easy and 50/100 hard cases, while B succeeds in 80/100 easy and 4/10 hard cases. A has a higher success rate in each group, but A is 59/110 overall and B is 84/110 because their group composition differs.
MCSE-202.distinction: A reversal signals that aggregation matters; it does not by itself identify a causal effect.

MCSE-202.title: Leakage and validation pipelines
MCSE-202.explanation: Leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time influences training or model selection. Fit preprocessing only on training partitions and keep a final test set separate.
MCSE-202.example: If the mean used for imputation is calculated using all records before a train–test split, test-set information has entered training.
MCSE-202.distinction: A random split can be misleading for temporal data; a chronological split may better match the deployment scenario.

MCSE-202.title: Bayesian updating and prior choice
MCSE-202.explanation: Bayesian inference combines a prior distribution with a likelihood to produce a posterior. A posterior predictive distribution incorporates uncertainty about model parameters in predictions.
MCSE-202.example: With a Beta(1,1) prior and 8 successes in 10 independent Bernoulli observations, the posterior is Beta(9,3).
MCSE-202.distinction: A posterior depends on the likelihood and prior; sensitivity checks can reveal when conclusions depend strongly on assumptions.

MCSE-202.title: Regression residuals and diagnostic plots
MCSE-202.explanation: A residual is observed outcome minus fitted outcome. Plotting residuals against fitted values or relevant predictors can reveal patterns, changing spread or outliers that suggest a model is inadequate; diagnostic results do not independently prove causation.
MCSE-202.example: If an observation is 12 and the model predicts 9, its residual is 3. A curved residual pattern across fitted values may indicate that a straight-line relationship is inadequate.
MCSE-202.distinction: A residual is computed from a fitted model; the unobserved population error is not generally available directly.

MCSE-202.title: Bayesian updating with a beta prior
MCSE-202.explanation: For independent Bernoulli trials with a common success probability p, a Beta(a,b) prior and s successes in n observations yield a Beta(a+s,b+n−s) posterior. This result follows from the chosen likelihood and prior and should not be applied when those assumptions are inappropriate.
MCSE-202.example: A Beta(1,1) prior updated with 8 successes and 2 failures becomes Beta(9,3), whose posterior mean is 9/12=0.75.
MCSE-202.distinction: A posterior mean is a model-based estimate; it should be reported with uncertainty and the assumptions that produced it.

MMLE-201.title: Big data and distributed systems
MMLE-201.explanation: Big data problems arise when volume, velocity, variety or processing needs exceed convenient single-machine approaches. Distributed systems split storage and computation across machines.
MMLE-201.example: A stream of device events can be partitioned and processed by multiple workers.
MMLE-201.distinction: More data is not automatically better: quality, governance, cost and bias still matter.

MMLE-201.title: Hadoop and HDFS
MMLE-201.explanation: Hadoop provides a distributed ecosystem; HDFS stores large files in blocks across machines and supports fault tolerance through replication. The NameNode manages metadata and DataNodes store blocks.
MMLE-201.example: A large file can be divided into blocks stored across several nodes; replicas help tolerate node failure.
MMLE-201.distinction: HDFS is designed for large-scale throughput; it is not a direct replacement for low-latency transactional storage.

MMLE-201.title: MapReduce and data movement
MMLE-201.explanation: MapReduce applies a map operation to input records, groups intermediate values by key, and reduces each group. Input ingestion and output retrieval form part of a complete pipeline.
MMLE-201.example: Word count emits (word,1) pairs in map and sums values for each word in reduce.
MMLE-201.distinction: Map transforms individual records; reduce aggregates values sharing a key.

MMLE-201.title: Hive and HiveQL
MMLE-201.explanation: Hive provides a SQL-like interface for querying data stored in a Hadoop environment. Tables describe schemas and queries are translated into execution plans.
MMLE-201.example: A HiveQL query can group event records by day and count rows per group.
MMLE-201.distinction: HiveQL resembles SQL but its execution and transaction features depend on the configured engine and storage.

MMLE-201.title: Pig and HBase
MMLE-201.explanation: Pig provides a data-flow language for transformations; HBase is a distributed, column-family-oriented database built for different access patterns than batch queries.
MMLE-201.example: A batch pipeline can transform logs before a serving system retrieves records by key.
MMLE-201.distinction: Hive is commonly used for analytic queries; HBase targets keyed access over large distributed tables.

MMLE-201.title: Spark and machine learning
MMLE-201.explanation: Spark processes distributed data with reusable computations and supports machine-learning workflows through Spark ML. H2O and Azure ML provide alternative tools or platforms named in the syllabus.
MMLE-201.example: Split data before fitting transformations, train a classifier and evaluate it on held-out records.
MMLE-201.distinction: Distributed training addresses scale, but does not by itself solve leakage, bias or poor evaluation.

MMLE-201.title: HDFS blocks and fault tolerance
MMLE-201.explanation: HDFS separates file-system metadata from data blocks. A configured replication factor creates copies on different nodes, and the system attempts recovery when a copy becomes unavailable.
MMLE-201.example: If the replication factor is 3, the system targets three replicas of each block subject to cluster conditions and placement policy.
MMLE-201.distinction: Replication improves availability but is not a substitute for an independent backup or protection from logical deletion.

MMLE-201.title: MapReduce word-count trace
MMLE-201.explanation: A mapper emits intermediate key–value pairs; the shuffle groups values by key; reducers aggregate each group. This separation allows work to be distributed.
MMLE-201.example: For “cat dog cat”, map emits (cat,1), (dog,1), (cat,1); shuffle groups cat:[1,1], dog:[1]; reduce emits cat:2 and dog:1.
MMLE-201.distinction: MapReduce is a programming model; Hadoop is an ecosystem that includes an implementation and storage components.

MMLE-201.title: Hive partitions and query design
MMLE-201.explanation: Partitioning organises data by selected fields so a query can skip irrelevant partitions when filtering. Tables may be managed or external depending on configuration and engine version.
MMLE-201.example: Partitioning event data by date can avoid reading other dates for a date-filtered query.
MMLE-201.distinction: Partitioning can improve targeted scans, but too many tiny partitions or files can add overhead.

MMLE-201.title: HDFS read path and failure handling
MMLE-201.explanation: An HDFS client asks the NameNode for metadata and block locations, then ordinarily transfers file data directly with suitable DataNodes. DataNodes report their status and blocks; replication and re-replication help the system tolerate failures subject to configuration.
MMLE-201.example: For a file stored in several blocks, a client obtains locations and reads the blocks from available DataNodes rather than routing all block data through the NameNode.
MMLE-201.distinction: Replication improves fault tolerance but does not replace a separately managed backup, particularly for accidental or malicious deletion.

MMLE-201.title: MapReduce shuffle and aggregation
MMLE-201.explanation: A map task emits intermediate key–value pairs. The framework partitions, transfers and groups values by key before reduce tasks process each group. Combiners can reduce transfer volume when their use is valid for the operation.
MMLE-201.example: For input “cat dog cat”, mapping emits (cat,1), (dog,1), (cat,1); after grouping, reducers sum cat:[1,1] to 2 and dog:[1] to 1.
MMLE-201.distinction: MapReduce defines a processing model; Hive is a query layer that can use different execution engines depending on deployment.

MMLC-301.title: Probability, Likelihood and Loss Formulations
MMLC-301.explanation: Deep learning replaces manual feature engineering with hierarchical representation learning across multiple processing layers. Probabilistic modeling forms the bedrock for defining objective functions: Bernoulli distributions model binary classification with Sigmoid outputs (P(X=x) = p^x (1-p)^(1-x)), Categorical distributions model multi-class classification with Softmax outputs (P(X=k) = p_k, sum p_k = 1), and Gaussian distributions derive Mean Squared Error under additive Gaussian noise assumptions. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) determines parameters theta by maximizing observed data probability, computed numerically via log-likelihood to prevent underflow: theta_MLE = argmax_theta sum_{i=1}^N log P(x^(i); theta).
MMLC-301.example:
Step-by-step MLE to Cross-Entropy Derivation:
1. Given independent binary targets y^(i) in {0, 1} with predicted probability y_hat^(i) = P(Y=1|x^(i); theta):
   L(theta) = prod_{i=1}^N (y_hat^(i))^(y^(i)) * (1 - y_hat^(i))^(1 - y^(i))
2. Take natural logarithm:
   log L(theta) = sum_{i=1}^N [y^(i) log y_hat^(i) + (1 - y^(i)) log(1 - y_hat^(i))]
3. Minimizing negative log-likelihood (NLL) normalized by sample count N yields Binary Cross-Entropy Loss:
   J_BCE = - (1/N) * sum_{i=1}^N [y^(i) log y_hat^(i) + (1 - y^(i)) log(1 - y_hat^(i))]
For multi-class categorical targets across C classes, this generalizes to Categorical Cross-Entropy:
   J_CCE = - sum_{i=1}^N sum_{c=1}^C y_{i,c} log(y_hat_{i,c}).
MMLC-301.distinction: Linear regression minimizes Mean Squared Error (MSE = (1/2N) sum (y - y_hat)^2) assuming continuous outputs with Gaussian noise; Logistic regression minimizes Cross-Entropy loss mapping projections to the [0, 1] probability simplex via sigmoid sigma(w^T x + b).

MMLC-301.title: Feed-Forward Networks, Universal Approximation and Activation Units
MMLC-301.explanation: Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) compose input signals through affine transformations and non-linear point-wise activations: a^(0) = x, z^(l) = W^(l) a^(l-1) + b^(l), a^(l) = g^(l)(z^(l)). If all activation functions g^(l) were linear, an L-layer network would collapse mathematically to a single matrix multiplication: y = W_L ... W_2 W_1 x = W_eff x, eliminating any depth representation. Non-linear activations enable networks with even a single hidden layer of sufficient width to approximate any continuous function over compact domains (Universal Approximation Theorem).
MMLC-301.example:
Activation Comparison & Behavior:
• Sigmoid: g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) in (0, 1). Saturates at both tails causing vanishing gradients; non-zero centered.
• Tanh: g(z) = (e^z - e^(-z)) / (e^z + e^(-z)) in (-1, 1). Zero-centered, but still suffers from saturation when |z| >> 0.
• ReLU: g(z) = max(0, z) in [0, +inf). Constant unit gradient for z > 0 accelerates convergence with zero saturation, but neurons can permanently die if z < 0 across all training data (Dying ReLU).
• Leaky ReLU: g(z) = max(0.01z, z) ensures a persistent gradient for negative inputs.
• Softmax: g(z_i) = e^(z_i) / sum_{j=1}^C e^(z_j) normalizes arbitrary real logits into a rigorous probability distribution summing to 1.
MMLC-301.distinction: Hidden layers use intermediate activations (ReLU, Leaky ReLU, Tanh) to build non-linear latent feature spaces; output layers use activations tailored to the task distribution (Linear for regression, Sigmoid for binary Bernoulli classification, Softmax for categorical multi-class classification).

MMLC-301.title: Backpropagation and Recursive Multivariate Chain Rule
MMLC-301.explanation: Backpropagation computes the exact partial derivatives of the scalar loss J with respect to every weight tensor W^(l) and bias vector b^(l) across all network layers by recursively propagating error signals backward from output layer L to input layer 1.
MMLC-301.example:
Recursive Delta Backpropagation Equations:
1. Output Layer Delta (l = L):
   delta^(L) = grad_{a^(L)} J (hadamard product) g'^(L)(z^(L))
   For Cross-Entropy with Softmax output: delta^(L) = y_hat - y (convenient numerical cancellation).
2. Hidden Layer Delta (l = L-1 down to 1):
   delta^(l) = ((W^(l+1))^T delta^(l+1)) (hadamard product) g'^(l)(z^(l))
3. Parameter Gradient Accumulation:
   del J / del W^(l) = delta^(l) * (a^(l-1))^T
   del J / del b^(l) = delta^(l)
4. Parameter Update via Gradient Descent:
   W^(l) <- W^(l) - alpha * (del J / del W^(l))
   b^(l) <- b^(l) - alpha * (del J / del b^(l)).
MMLC-301.distinction: Forward propagation maps inputs to activations and computes the scalar objective J; backward propagation caches activation vectors and recursively applies transposed weight matrices to compute gradients in O(parameters) time rather than O(parameters^2).

MMLC-301.title: Generalisation, Regularisation and Bias-Variance Mechanics
MMLC-301.explanation: Total expected generalization error decomposes into Bias^2 + Variance + Irreducible Noise. High bias indicates model underfitting (failure to capture underlying patterns); high variance indicates overfitting (sensitivity to training sample noise). Regularization constraints network capacity to minimize test error.
MMLC-301.example:
Mechanics of Regularization Techniques:
• L2 Regularization (Weight Decay): Adds (lambda / 2N) sum ||w||^2 to the loss. Weight update becomes W <- W * (1 - alpha * lambda / N) - alpha * grad J, shrinking weights exponentially toward zero to penalize explosive parameters.
• L1 Regularization (Lasso): Adds (lambda / N) sum |w| to the loss, driving non-essential weights to exact zero and inducing architectural sparsity.
• Dropout: At each training step, neurons are randomly set to zero with probability p (typically 0.2 to 0.5), preventing co-adaptation of features. At test time, all neurons remain active with weights multiplied by (1-p) for inverted scaling.
• Early Stopping: Monitors validation loss and halts optimization before overtraining occurs.
MMLC-301.distinction: L2 regularization smoothly shrinks all weights towards zero preserving dense representations; L1 regularization creates true coordinate zeros for feature selection.

MMLC-301.title: Convolutional Neural Networks: Receptive Fields and Spatial Dimensions
MMLC-301.explanation: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) process grid-structured topological data (e.g., 2D images, audio spectrograms) by leveraging three core architectural principles: sparse local receptive fields, parameter sharing (tying kernel weights across spatial locations), and translation equivariance (f(g(x)) = g(f(x))).
MMLC-301.example:
Spatial Output Dimension Formula:
Given input spatial size W, kernel filter size K, zero-padding P, and stride S, the output spatial dimension O is given by:
   O = floor((W - K + 2P) / S) + 1
Numerical Calculation:
Input image = 32x32, Kernel = 5x5, Padding P = 2, Stride S = 1:
   O = floor((32 - 5 + 2*2) / 1) + 1 = floor(31 / 1) + 1 = 32 (Same-padding preserves spatial resolution).
If Stride S = 2 without padding (P = 0):
   O = floor((32 - 5 + 0) / 2) + 1 = floor(27 / 2) + 1 = 13 + 1 = 14x14 output feature map.
MMLC-301.distinction: Fully connected layers require a unique parameter for every input-output coordinate pair, scaling quadratically with spatial resolution; convolutional layers share kernel weights across the entire feature plane, making them parameter-efficient and translation-equivariant.

MMLC-301.title: Recurrent Neural Networks, Sequence Models and LSTM Gating Architecture
MMLC-301.explanation: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process sequential sequences by maintaining a continuous recurrent hidden state: h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + W_xh x_t + b). However, backpropagating through long sequences causes repeated matrix multiplications by W_hh, triggering catastrophic exponential vanishing or exploding gradients.
MMLC-301.example:
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Additive Highway Equations:
LSTMs resolve vanishing gradients by introducing an internal constant error carousel (cell state C_t) regulated by 4 multiplicative gates:
1. Forget Gate: f_t = sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) in [0, 1] (decides what historical memory to discard)
2. Input Gate: i_t = sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i) (decides which candidate values to store)
3. Candidate Cell State: C_tilde_t = tanh(W_c [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c)
4. Cell State Update: C_t = f_t (hadamard) C_{t-1} + i_t (hadamard) C_tilde_t (additive highway preserves long gradients!)
5. Output Gate: o_t = sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o)
6. Final Hidden State: h_t = o_t (hadamard) tanh(C_t).
MMLC-301.distinction: Standard RNNs multiply hidden states recursively at every step leading to vanishing gradients; LSTMs perform additive updates to cell state C_t, allowing error gradients to propagate across hundreds of time steps unattenuated.

MMLC-301.title: Autoencoders: Bottleneck Latent Spaces and Taxonomy
MMLC-301.explanation: Autoencoders are self-supervised neural architectures designed to compress high-dimensional inputs x into a lower-dimensional bottleneck latent representation z, and subsequently reconstruct the input as x_hat with minimal distortion loss ||x - x_hat||^2.
MMLC-301.example:
Autoencoder Taxonomy & Mechanics:
• Undercomplete AE: Latent dimensionality dim(z) < dim(x). Compels the network to discover the most salient non-linear manifold features.
• Denoising AE (DAE): Corrupts raw input with noise x_tilde ~ q(x_tilde|x) and trains the network to reconstruct the original clean x, preventing identity shortcut mapping.
• Sparse AE: Penalizes non-zero activations in an overcomplete latent space (dim(z) > dim(x)) using L1 or Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence penalty.
• Variational Autoencoder (VAE): Maps inputs probabilistically to parameters of a distribution (mean mu(x) and log-variance sigma^2(x)), optimized via the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) with the reparameterization trick z = mu + sigma * epsilon where epsilon ~ N(0, I).
MMLC-301.distinction: Deterministic autoencoders map inputs to fixed discrete latent vectors which can leave gaps in the latent space; Variational Autoencoders map inputs to continuous probability distributions, allowing smooth generative sampling.

MMLC-301.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) vs Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
MMLC-301.explanation: Deep generative modeling aims to estimate and sample from complex unknown probability distributions p_data(x). VAEs adopt an explicit probabilistic formulation, whereas GANs utilize an adversarial game-theoretic formulation without explicit density estimation.
MMLC-301.example:
GAN Minimax Formulation:
A Generator G(z; theta_g) and a Discriminator D(x; theta_d) compete in a zero-sum game:
   min_G max_D V(D, G) = E_{x~p_data}[log D(x)] + E_{z~p_z}[log(1 - D(G(z)))]
• Discriminator Goal: Maximize log D(x) for real samples and log(1 - D(G(z))) for generated samples.
• Generator Goal: Minimize log(1 - D(G(z))) (or maximize log D(G(z)) to prevent early training vanishing gradients).
Comparison Matrix:
• Objective: VAE maximizes ELBO (Reconstruction + KL Divergence); GAN solves a zero-sum minimax saddle point.
• Output Quality: VAEs produce slightly blurry images due to pixel-space L2/MSE loss; GANs produce crisp, highly realistic samples.
• Training Stability: VAE training is stable and convex in latent parameters; GANs suffer from mode collapse, oscillations, and vanishing gradients.
MMLC-301.distinction: VAEs provide tractable approximate inference and a structured latent space at the cost of blurriness; GANs produce sharper images but offer no direct inference or latent representation inversion.

MMLC-301.title: Transfer Learning Strategies and Fine-Tuning Protocols
MMLC-301.explanation: Transfer learning leverages deep representations acquired from massive benchmark corpora (e.g., ImageNet, LAION, Wikipedia) and adapts them to specialized downstream target tasks where annotated data is scarce.
MMLC-301.example:
Transfer Strategy Decision Matrix:
1. Small Target Dataset + High Similarity to Pre-training Domain:
   Strategy: Freeze pre-trained convolutional/transformer backbone; train only the linear output classification head. Prevents catastrophic overfitting.
2. Small Target Dataset + Low Similarity:
   Strategy: Train high-level layers and output head; freeze only initial fundamental edge/texture filters. (Challenging; data augmentation is vital).
3. Large Target Dataset + High/Low Similarity:
   Strategy: Full Model Fine-Tuning. Initialize with pre-trained weights and fine-tune all layers using a small learning rate (e.g., alpha = 1e-4 or 1e-5 with warmup and cosine decay) so learned features are gently adapted without destroying pre-trained representations.
MMLC-301.distinction: Feature extraction keeps pre-trained backbone weights strictly frozen; fine-tuning updates backbone weights with conservative learning rates.

MMLC-301.title: Deep Belief Networks and Stacked Restricted Boltzmann Machines
MMLC-301.explanation: Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) are deep probabilistic graphical models composed of multiple layers of stochastic latent variables. The top two layers form an undirected bipartite Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM), while lower layers form a directed generative graph.
MMLC-301.example:
Layer-Wise Greedy Pre-training Protocol:
1. Step 1: Train RBM 1 on raw data vectors x in an unsupervised fashion using Contrastive Divergence (CD-k).
2. Step 2: Freeze RBM 1 weights W_1, compute hidden probabilities h_1, and treat h_1 as visible training inputs for RBM 2.
3. Step 3: Repeat layer by layer to stack representations without requiring target labels.
4. Step 4: Add a supervised linear or softmax classification layer on top, then fine-tune all layer parameters globally using supervised backpropagation.
MMLC-301.distinction: Classical deep networks trained from scratch with random initialization suffered from vanishing gradients; DBN greedy layer-wise pre-training placed network weights in a basins of attraction prior to gradient descent.

MMLC-301.title: Practical Hardware Optimization and Numerical Stability
MMLC-301.explanation: Deploying deep learning in practice demands disciplined attention to hardware acceleration (CUDA tensor cores, mixed precision), gradient stability, and numerical safeguards.
MMLC-301.example:
Essential Engineering Safeguards:
1. Gradient Clipping: If ||grad J|| > threshold c, re-scale: grad <- (c / ||grad J||) * grad to prevent catastrophic exploding gradients.
2. Mixed Precision (FP16/BF16): Performs matrix multiplications in 16-bit floating point while storing master weights in FP32, reducing GPU memory footprint by 50% and doubling tensor throughput.
3. Log-Sum-Exp Trick: Evaluates log(sum e^{z_i}) as c + log(sum e^{z_i - c}) where c = max(z_i) to prevent numerical overflow in Softmax and Cross-Entropy computations.
4. Learning Rate Schedules: Warmup for the first 5% of training steps followed by Cosine Annealing to smoothly converge to local minima.
MMLC-301.distinction: Vanishing gradients make weights stop learning; exploding gradients cause NaN loss values and arithmetic overflow.

MMLE-302.title: The RL Interaction Loop, Return and Discounting Mechanics
MMLE-302.explanation: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a mathematical framework for learning optimal sequential decision making through environmental feedback. An agent observes state S_t, selects action A_t according to policy pi, receives scalar reward R_{t+1}, and transitions to next state S_{t+1}. Unlike supervised learning (where correct target labels are given), RL receives delayed, evaluative scalar feedback. The goal is to maximize the cumulative return G_t = sum_{k=0}^inf gamma^k R_{t+k+1}, where discount factor gamma in [0, 1) ensures infinite-horizon convergence and balances immediate versus far-future rewards.
MMLE-302.example:
Return Calculation Example:
Given gamma = 0.9 and an agent receives rewards R_1 = -1, R_2 = 0, R_3 = +10, R_4 = 0 (terminal):
• Return from t=0:
   G_0 = R_1 + gamma * R_2 + gamma^2 * R_3 = -1 + 0.9*(0) + (0.9)^2 * 10 = -1 + 0 + 8.1 = +7.1.
If gamma = 0 (myopic/greedy):
   G_0 = R_1 = -1.
If gamma = 1 (undiscounted):
   G_0 = -1 + 0 + 10 = +9.0.
MMLE-302.distinction: Reward R_{t+1} is the immediate scalar feedback received at step t+1; Return G_t is the accumulated discounted future reward over the entire subsequent trajectory.

MMLE-302.title: Markov Decision Processes, POMDPs and the Markov Property
MMLE-302.explanation: A stochastic process possesses the Markov Property if the conditional probability distribution of future states depends solely upon the present state and action, independent of preceding history: P(S_{t+1} | S_t, A_t, ..., S_0, A_0) = P(S_{t+1} | S_t, A_t). A Markov Decision Process (MDP) is formally defined by the tuple (S, A, P, R, gamma). When the environment state is only partially observed through sensor measurements O_t, the system is modeled as a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP), where the agent must maintain a belief state distribution b(s) = P(S_t = s | history).
MMLE-302.example:
MDP Tuple Components:
• S: Set of all valid environment states.
• A: Set of valid actions (may be state-dependent A(s)).
• P(s' | s, a) = Pr(S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s, A_t = a): State transition probability matrix.
• R(s, a) = E[R_{t+1} | S_t = s, A_t = a]: Expected reward function.
• gamma in [0, 1): Discount factor.
MMLE-302.distinction: In a fully observable MDP, the current state S_t is a sufficient statistic for optimal decision making; in a POMDP, observation O_t is incomplete, requiring history or belief state tracking.

MMLE-302.title: Value Functions, Advantage and Bellman Expectation Equations
MMLE-302.explanation: Value functions quantify the long-term desirability of states and state-action pairs under a policy pi. The state-value function V^pi(s) = E_pi[G_t | S_t = s] evaluates states; the action-value function Q^pi(s, a) = E_pi[G_t | S_t = s, A_t = a] evaluates actions. The Advantage function A^pi(s, a) = Q^pi(s, a) - V^pi(s) quantifies how much better action a is compared to the default expected policy return.
MMLE-302.example:
Recursive Bellman Expectation Equations:
• For State Value V^pi(s):
   V^pi(s) = sum_{a in A} pi(a|s) sum_{s' in S} P(s'|s, a) [ R(s, a, s') + gamma * V^pi(s') ]
• For Action Value Q^pi(s, a):
   Q^pi(s, a) = sum_{s' in S} P(s'|s, a) [ R(s, a, s') + gamma * sum_{a' in A} pi(a'|s') Q^pi(s', a') ]
Numerical Example:
If an action yields immediate reward r = -1, leads to next state s' with V(s') = 5, and gamma = 0.9:
   Backed-up Value = -1 + 0.9 * (5) = +3.5.
MMLE-302.distinction: V^pi(s) averages values over all actions chosen by policy pi; Q^pi(s, a) evaluates taking a specific first action a and then following policy pi thereafter.

MMLE-302.title: Bellman Optimality Equations and Dynamic Programming Planning
MMLE-302.explanation: The optimal value function V*(s) = max_pi V^pi(s) represents the maximum expected return achievable from state s. Dynamic programming (DP) algorithms assume complete knowledge of the MDP transition matrix P and reward function R, solving for optimal behavior through recursive backups without live trial-and-error.
MMLE-302.example:
Bellman Optimality Equations:
• V*(s) = max_{a in A} sum_{s' in S} P(s'|s, a) [ R(s, a, s') + gamma * V*(s') ]
• Q*(s, a) = sum_{s' in S} P(s'|s, a) [ R(s, a, s') + gamma * max_{a' in A} Q*(s', a') ]
Policy Iteration vs Value Iteration:
• Policy Iteration (PI): Alternates full Policy Evaluation (solving V_k+1(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) sum_s' P[R + gamma V_k]) until convergence, followed by Policy Improvement (pi'(s) = argmax_a sum_s' P[R + gamma V]). Reaches exact optimal policy in finitely many sweeps.
• Value Iteration (VI): Combines evaluation and improvement into a single Bellman optimality backup: V_{k+1}(s) = max_a sum_s' P(s'|s, a)[R + gamma V_k(s')]. Sweeps stop when max_s |V_{k+1}(s) - V_k(s)| < epsilon.
MMLE-302.distinction: Policy iteration explicitly computes and updates a distinct policy at each outer loop; value iteration updates state values directly using the max operator and extracts the greedy policy only at termination.

MMLE-302.title: Model-Free Evaluation: Monte Carlo vs Temporal-Difference Learning
MMLE-302.explanation: When environment dynamics P and R are unknown, the agent must estimate value functions from sampled interaction trajectories. Monte Carlo (MC) methods learn from completed episode returns G_t, whereas Temporal-Difference (TD) methods bootstrap using successor state value estimates after each individual transition.
MMLE-302.example:
Update Equations:
• Monte Carlo (MC): V(S_t) <- V(S_t) + alpha * [G_t - V(S_t)]
  Requires waiting until the terminal state to compute full return G_t. Target is unbiased but exhibits high variance.
• Temporal-Difference TD(0): V(S_t) <- V(S_t) + alpha * [R_{t+1} + gamma * V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)]
  Where delta_t = R_{t+1} + gamma * V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t) is the TD Error. Updates online transition-by-transition. Introduces estimation bias but drastically reduces variance.
MMLE-302.distinction: Monte Carlo does not bootstrap (evaluates true sample return G_t after episode ends); TD(0) bootstraps immediately from the estimated successor value V(S_{t+1}) without waiting for episode termination.

MMLE-302.title: Model-Free Control: SARSA vs Q-Learning with Worked Numerical Update
MMLE-302.explanation: Control algorithms discover optimal policies without an explicit world model. SARSA is an on-policy TD control method that updates Q using the action actually executed by the behavior policy. Q-learning is an off-policy TD control method that updates Q toward the maximum achievable action value regardless of which action was executed.
MMLE-302.example:
Step-by-Step Numerical Comparison:
Suppose current state-action value Q(s, a) = 2.0, immediate reward r = 1.0, discount gamma = 0.9, learning rate alpha = 0.5. At successor state s', the available action values are Q(s', left) = 4.0 and Q(s', right) = 6.0. An exploratory behavior policy chooses action A' = left.

1. Q-Learning Update (Off-Policy):
   Target Y_Q = r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') = 1.0 + 0.9 * max(4.0, 6.0) = 1.0 + 0.9 * 6.0 = 6.4
   New Q(s, a) = 2.0 + 0.5 * (6.4 - 2.0) = 2.0 + 0.5 * (4.4) = 4.20.

2. SARSA Update (On-Policy):
   Target Y_SARSA = r + gamma * Q(s', A'=left) = 1.0 + 0.9 * (4.0) = 1.0 + 3.6 = 4.6
   New Q(s, a) = 2.0 + 0.5 * (4.6 - 2.0) = 2.0 + 0.5 * (2.6) = 3.30.

Conclusion: Q-learning evaluates the optimal greedy target (6.0) yielding Q = 4.20; SARSA evaluates the actual exploratory action taken (left, value 4.0) yielding Q = 3.30.
MMLE-302.distinction: Q-learning directly learns Q* for the greedy optimal policy while exploring (off-policy); SARSA learns the action-value function for the behavior policy including its exploratory mistakes (on-policy, learning safer paths in Cliff Walking).

MMLE-302.title: Deep Q-Networks (DQN), Replay Buffers and Double DQN
MMLE-302.explanation: Tabular Q-learning cannot scale to high-dimensional state spaces (e.g., raw pixels or continuous kinematics). Deep Q-Networks (DQN) parameterize Q(s, a; theta) with deep neural networks. Standard training destabilizes due to the "Deadly Triad": combining function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy updates.
MMLE-302.example:
DQN Stabilization Mechanisms:
1. Experience Replay Buffer D: Stores transitions (s_t, a_t, r_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, done). Random minibatch sampling breaks temporal correlation and prevents catastrophic forgetting.
2. Target Network Q(s, a; theta^-): Maintains a frozen copy of weights theta^- updated periodically (every C steps) to provide stable regression targets:
   y = r + gamma * (1 - done) * max_{a'} Q(s', a'; theta^-)
   Loss L(theta) = Huber_loss(y - Q(s, a; theta)).
3. Double DQN: Standard DQN overestimates Q-values due to the max operator. Double DQN decouples action selection from action evaluation:
   y_Double = r + gamma * Q(s', argmax_{a'} Q(s', a'; theta); theta^-).
MMLE-302.distinction: Standard DQN uses the same target network weights to both pick and evaluate the maximum action; Double DQN uses the online network to select the best action and the target network to evaluate its value, eliminating overestimation bias.

MMLE-302.title: Policy Search, REINFORCE and Actor-Critic Architectures
MMLE-302.explanation: Policy gradient methods parameterize policy pi_theta(a|s) directly and maximize expected return J(theta) = E_{tau ~ pi_theta}[G_0] via gradient ascent theta <- theta + alpha * grad_theta J(theta). By the Policy Gradient Theorem, the gradient can be computed without differentiating environmental transition dynamics: grad_theta J(theta) = E[ sum_t grad_theta log pi_theta(A_t | S_t) * G_t ].
MMLE-302.example:
Policy Gradient Algorithms:
• REINFORCE: Monte Carlo policy gradient. Samples complete trajectories, computes return-to-go G_t = sum_{k=t}^T gamma^{k-t} R_{k+1}, and updates: theta <- theta + alpha * sum_t grad_theta log pi_theta(A_t|S_t) * (G_t - b(S_t)). Subtracting state baseline b(S_t) = V(S_t) drastically reduces gradient variance without introducing bias.
• Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C/A3C): Replaces high-variance return G_t with a 1-step TD advantage estimate A(S_t, A_t) = R_{t+1} + gamma * V_w(S_{t+1}) - V_w(S_t). The Actor updates policy parameters theta; the Critic updates value parameters w.
• Modern Continuous Control: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) clips probability ratios r_t(theta) to prevent destructive policy updates; SAC (Soft Actor-Critic) maximizes entropy alongside reward.
MMLE-302.distinction: Value-based methods select actions implicitly via argmax Q(s, a), struggling with continuous high-dimensional actions; policy-based methods directly output action probabilities or Gaussian distribution parameters (mu, sigma).

MMLE-302.title: Imitation Learning: Behavior Cloning, DAgger, IRL and GAIL
MMLE-302.explanation: When rewards are sparse, expensive, or dangerous to discover through random exploration, imitation learning leverages expert demonstration trajectories D_demo = {(s_i, a_i)} to train policies.
MMLE-302.example:
Taxonomy of Imitation Learning Paradigms:
• Behavior Cloning (BC): Supervised learning mapping states to expert actions: theta* = argmin_theta E_{(s,a)~D}[ -log pi_theta(a|s) ]. Vulnerable to Covariate Shift / Compounding Errors: minor execution deviations place the agent into unobserved states where it fails catastrophically.
• DAgger (Dataset Aggregation): Interleaves learner execution with expert re-labeling. The learner visits states, queries the expert for correct actions on those visited states, aggregates them into dataset D, and retrains, eliminating distribution shift.
• Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL): Recovers the underlying reward function R*(s, a) that rationalizes the expert demonstrations, then trains an RL agent on R*.
• GAIL (Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning): Uses a GAN-like discriminator D(s, a) to distinguish expert transitions from agent transitions, training policy pi to fool the discriminator.
MMLE-302.distinction: Behavior cloning is simple supervised learning that breaks down under distribution drift; DAgger queries an interactive expert on newly visited states to guarantee robust covariate coverage.

MMLE-302.title: Exploration Strategies: Epsilon-Greedy, UCB, and Thompson Sampling
MMLE-302.explanation: The exploration-exploitation trade-off balances exploiting current value estimates to maximize immediate performance versus exploring untried actions to reduce epistemic uncertainty and discover superior long-term policies.
MMLE-302.example:
Exploration Mechanics:
• Fixed vs Decaying Epsilon-Greedy: Selects argmax Q with probability 1 - epsilon and uniform random action with probability epsilon. Decaying epsilon over episodes (e.g., epsilon_t = max(epsilon_min, epsilon_0 * exp(-decay * t))) explores broadly early on and exploits later.
• Upper Confidence Bound (UCB1): Balances value estimates with confidence intervals:
   a_t = argmax_{a in A} [ Q_bar(a) + c * sqrt( ln(t) / N_t(a) ) ]
   The exploration bonus c * sqrt(ln(t) / N_t(a)) shrinks as an action is repeatedly selected, implementing optimism in the face of uncertainty.
• Thompson Sampling: Maintains a Bayesian posterior distribution over action rewards and selects action a according to its posterior probability of being optimal.
• Entropy Regularization: In policy gradients, adds beta * H(pi_theta(.|s)) to the objective, penalizing premature deterministic collapse.
MMLE-302.distinction: Epsilon-greedy explores purely randomly with uniform probability across all alternative actions; UCB directs exploration purposefully toward actions with high uncertainty.

MMLE-302.title: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), UCT and AlphaZero Paradigm
MMLE-302.explanation: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a heuristic planning algorithm for vast decision spaces (such as Go, Chess, and complex robotics) that selectively grows a search tree guided by simulation outcomes.
MMLE-302.example:
The Four MCTS Standard Phases:
1. Selection: Starting from root state s_0, recursively traverses tree nodes using the UCT (Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees) formula until reaching an expandable leaf node:
   UCT(s, a) = Q_bar(s, a) + c * sqrt( ln N(s) / N(s, a) )
2. Expansion: Adds one or more untried child nodes corresponding to legal successor actions.
3. Simulation (Rollout): Simulates the remainder of the episode using a fast default rollout policy (or evaluates the leaf using a trained neural network value head V_theta(s)).
4. Backpropagation: Propagates the terminal outcome reward z up the selected path, updating visit counts N(s) <- N(s) + 1 and running mean values Q_bar(s, a) <- Q_bar(s, a) + (z - Q_bar(s, a)) / N(s, a).
AlphaZero Enhancement: Replaces random rollouts with a dual-head policy-value network (p, v) = f_theta(s) and uses PUCT: UCT(s, a) = Q(s, a) + c_puct * P(s, a) * sqrt(sum_b N(s, b)) / (1 + N(s, a)).
MMLE-302.distinction: Dynamic programming sweeps exhaustively across all states and actions; MCTS builds an asymmetric tree allocating compute power exclusively to promising trajectories.

MCSC-106.title: Defining an independent study
MCSC-106.explanation: Start with a manageable topic and formulate a question whose scope can be investigated with the time and resources available. Agree goals and milestones with a supervisor.
MCSC-106.example: Replace “study AI security” with a focused question about one clearly defined threat and setting.
MCSC-106.distinction: A topic names an area; a research question states what you intend to investigate.

MCSC-106.title: Finding and assessing sources
MCSC-106.explanation: Search scholarly databases, trace references and evaluate relevance, methods, limitations and publication context. Keep a record of search terms and decisions.
MCSC-106.example: Create a literature matrix listing problem, data, method, result and limitation for each paper.
MCSC-106.distinction: A literature review synthesises and compares sources rather than merely listing abstracts.

MCSC-106.title: Research integrity and progress
MCSC-106.explanation: Record methods and sources, cite borrowed work, retain reproducible notes and report uncertainty. Confirm progress and submission requirements with your supervisor.
MCSC-106.example: Maintain a dated log of experiments, code versions, observations and next steps.
MCSC-106.distinction: A preliminary result is evidence to examine, not a conclusion that must be defended regardless of contrary data.

MCSC-106.title: Search strategies and evidence tables
MCSC-106.explanation: Build a search using concept blocks joined with AND and synonyms joined with OR. Record databases, dates, exact queries and selection criteria so the search can be revisited.
MCSC-106.example: A query might combine (phishing OR fraudulent website) with (detection OR classification); screen title and abstract against a defined question.
MCSC-106.distinction: A systematic search follows a documented process; a narrative overview may be broader and less reproducible.

MCSC-106.title: Research questions and operational definitions
MCSC-106.explanation: A useful question defines the setting, variables and intended comparison. An operational definition states how an abstract construct will be observed or measured.
MCSC-106.example: Define detection latency as elapsed time between an event arriving and a decision being produced, measured by a specified clock and protocol.
MCSC-106.distinction: A conceptual definition explains meaning; an operational definition explains measurement.

MCSC-106.title: Search strategy and screening record
MCSC-106.explanation: Identify a research question, list synonyms for its key concepts, and search suitable scholarly databases. Record the database, exact query, search date, filters, screening criteria and reasons for exclusion. Backward and forward citation searches can identify additional relevant sources.
MCSC-106.example: A search can combine (phishing OR fraudulent website) AND (detection OR classification), then screen results against a predeclared scope and document the decision.
MCSC-106.distinction: A broad scoping search helps learn the field; a systematic review requires a documented protocol and suitable, transparent screening.

MCSC-106.title: Evaluating evidence and research gaps
MCSC-106.explanation: A literature matrix can compare each paper’s problem, data, method, evaluation and limitations. A credible gap emerges from a synthesis of relevant work and should be stated at an appropriate level of certainty; a small matrix cannot establish that nobody has ever addressed the issue.
MCSC-106.example: If several reviewed studies evaluate on one dataset, a possible question is how their methods perform across additional datasets; check the broader literature before asserting novelty.
MCSC-106.distinction: A claim that a gap exists needs evidence from actual sources; fictional examples illustrate the method only.

MCSC-202.title: Developing the research plan
MCSC-202.explanation: Refine a research question, review prior work and justify a method appropriate to the question. Define measurable outcomes and a feasible timetable with your supervisor.
MCSC-202.example: For a classification study, specify the dataset, baseline, split, metrics and intended analysis before training.
MCSC-202.distinction: A research objective states the aim; a method explains how evidence will be gathered.

MCSC-202.title: Pilot and evaluation
MCSC-202.explanation: A pilot checks feasibility and can expose data, measurement or implementation problems before a full study. Document changes rather than treating exploratory decisions as preplanned.
MCSC-202.example: Run a small pipeline end to end to detect missing labels and estimate processing time.
MCSC-202.distinction: A pilot checks the process; a final evaluation supports the study’s conclusions.

MCSC-202.title: Ethics and reproducibility
MCSC-202.explanation: Consider consent, privacy, data rights, security and the limitations of any available sample. Record versions and assumptions so results can be checked.
MCSC-202.example: Store only needed data and explain any permissions or approval required by the institution.
MCSC-202.distinction: Reproducibility of a computation does not by itself establish that its data or conclusions are valid.

MCSC-202.title: Research designs and baselines
MCSC-202.explanation: Choose an observational, experimental, simulation or other design according to the question, available resources and ethical constraints. Define a baseline that makes the proposed contribution meaningful.
MCSC-202.example: A system comparison can use the same dataset and evaluation split for both a proposed model and a simple existing baseline.
MCSC-202.distinction: A baseline is a reference for comparison; a control condition is defined by an experimental design.

MCSC-202.title: Pilot studies and protocol changes
MCSC-202.explanation: A pilot checks whether recruitment, instruments, data handling or code are workable. Record changes made after the pilot and distinguish planned from exploratory analysis.
MCSC-202.example: A pilot of ten sample records may reveal malformed timestamps before the full data pipeline is run.
MCSC-202.distinction: A successful pilot does not guarantee adequate statistical power or unbiased results in the full study.

MCSC-202.title: Pilot design and stopping criteria
MCSC-202.explanation: A pilot evaluates whether an intended procedure is feasible: data access, recruitment, measurement, runtime and safety should be checked against pre-specified criteria where practical. Record deviations and changes, including how pilot data will be handled in the full study.
MCSC-202.example: A pilot processes a small sample through collection, preprocessing and reporting, revealing that some timestamps are missing; the protocol is revised and the change recorded.
MCSC-202.distinction: A pilot can reveal practical problems but does not establish adequate power or unbiased effects in a full study.

MCSC-202.title: Baselines and reproducible comparison
MCSC-202.explanation: Choose a simple baseline and relevant established methods suited to the research question. Keep comparisons fair by stating data splits, resources, tuning budgets, metrics and uncertainty; record code, versions and random seeds where relevant.
MCSC-202.example: When comparing two classifiers, use the same predefined test split and report their training and tuning procedures as well as precision and recall.
MCSC-202.distinction: A proposed approach need not outperform every baseline for the study to be useful; transparent negative results can be informative.

MCSC-302.title: Dissertation I: proposal and literature
MCSC-302.explanation: Define a focused research problem, review the literature and show the gap your proposed work addresses. Agree the scope and institutional milestones with your supervisor.
MCSC-302.example: A proposal can state the problem, motivation, research questions, method, resources and expected evaluation.
MCSC-302.distinction: A research gap is an evidence-backed limitation in prior work, not simply an area with many publications.

MCSC-302.title: Method and feasibility
MCSC-302.explanation: Select data, baselines, metrics and an analysis plan suited to the question; check practical, ethical and access constraints. Use a pilot to assess feasibility.
MCSC-302.example: Before an experiment, define a train–validation–test separation and a baseline appropriate to the task.
MCSC-302.distinction: A feasibility result supports a plan; it is not necessarily the final study result.

MCSC-302.title: Documenting progress
MCSC-302.explanation: Maintain versioned code and data references, document assumptions and report deviations from the plan. Departmental rules determine the precise submission and review process.
MCSC-302.example: Keep a research log and a short progress report describing work completed, evidence, issues and next steps.
MCSC-302.distinction: A milestone is a planning aid; formal assessment requirements come from your institution.

MCSC-302.title: Literature synthesis and research gap
MCSC-302.explanation: Compare previous studies by problem, dataset, method, evaluation and limitations. Define a gap that follows from that comparison and a question that can be addressed with available evidence.
MCSC-302.example: If published models are tested only on one dataset, a proposed study might evaluate generalisation across clearly identified datasets, subject to access and comparability.
MCSC-302.distinction: A topic is a broad area; a gap is a specific supported limitation or unresolved question.

MCSC-302.title: Methodology and study protocol
MCSC-302.explanation: Specify data provenance, inclusion rules, preprocessing, baselines, outcome measures, analysis and ethical safeguards before conducting the study where feasible.
MCSC-302.example: A classification protocol can define dataset versions, leakage-resistant splits, baseline models, metrics and a plan for handling failures.
MCSC-302.distinction: A pilot checks whether a procedure works; it does not guarantee that the full study is unbiased or adequately powered.

MCSC-302.title: Research objectives and operationalisation
MCSC-302.explanation: A dissertation objective should be answerable with the chosen evidence and feasible within the available time and resources. Operationalisation translates important constructs into measurable or otherwise observable indicators, with units and procedures stated where appropriate.
MCSC-302.example: For a system-performance objective, specify workload, measurement hardware, latency definition and a baseline before making a comparison.
MCSC-302.distinction: A research objective states what the study seeks to learn; a performance metric states how one aspect of a system is measured.

MCSC-302.title: Limitations, evidence and dissertation claims
MCSC-302.explanation: Document the boundaries of the data, method, measurement and evaluation. Relate conclusions to the design and avoid presenting a dataset-specific result as universally valid. Follow the supervisor’s and university’s current dissertation requirements.
MCSC-302.example: A model evaluated on one institution’s data may not generalise to other institutions; name that limit and, where possible, propose an independent external evaluation.
MCSC-302.distinction: A limitation qualifies what the evidence supports; it does not automatically invalidate a carefully scoped result.

MCSC-401.title: Dissertation II: execution and analysis
MCSC-401.explanation: Carry out the agreed study, record procedures and analyse results against the research questions. Clearly separate planned analyses from exploratory findings.
MCSC-401.example: Compare a proposed method with specified baselines on the same evaluation protocol and report uncertainty where appropriate.
MCSC-401.distinction: A measured improvement is not automatically evidence of causation or real-world usefulness.

MCSC-401.title: Writing and presentation
MCSC-401.explanation: A dissertation commonly presents the problem, related work, methods, results, discussion, limitations and references. Follow your department’s current formatting and submission requirements.
MCSC-401.example: A results section reports observations; a discussion interprets their meaning and limitations.
MCSC-401.distinction: Results describe what was observed; discussion explains implications without overstating them.

MCSC-401.title: Reproducibility and final checks
MCSC-401.explanation: Verify citations, figure permissions, data handling, calculations and reproducibility. Document what can and cannot be shared and secure any necessary approvals.
MCSC-401.example: Record software versions, dataset provenance, configuration and steps needed to rerun an analysis.
MCSC-401.distinction: Reproducible code supports checking, but valid design and representative data remain separate requirements.

MCSC-102.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ rule
MCSC-102.explanation: Conditional probability updates an event probability when another event is known: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Bayes’ rule reverses the conditioning using a prior and likelihood.
MCSC-102.example: If P(A)=0.2, P(B|A)=0.8 and P(B|not A)=0.1, then P(B)=0.24 and P(A|B)=2/3.
MCSC-102.distinction: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; independent events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).

MCSC-102.title: Estimation, confidence intervals and tests
